stem: A 15-year-old boy comes to the office due to 4 weeks of left groin and thigh pain.  The dull, aching pain is exacerbated by activity.  He has been unable to participate in school physical activities over the last week due to worsening pain.  The patient reports no trauma, fever, chills, pain in other joints, or rashes.  He has no prior medical conditions and takes no medications.  Vital signs are normal.  BMI is at the 95th percentile.  At rest, the left leg is externally rotated.  There is tenderness of the left anterior hip, and passive range of motion of the left hip is limited due to pain, particularly with internal rotation.  The gait is antalgic.  The remainder of the physical examination is normal.  Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​

explanation:
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

Pathophysiology

  • Excessive shearing forces at proximal femoral physis → displacement of proximal femur diaphysis
  • Risk factors: obesity, adolescence

Clinical presentation

  • Hip pain
  • Referred groin, thigh, or knee pain
  • Altered gait
  • Limited internal rotation of hip

Diagnosis

  • X-ray: anterosuperior displaced femoral neck relative to femoral head

This adolescent with obesity (BMI ≥95th percentile) has chronic groin pain and limited internal rotation of the hip, findings concerning for slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).

SCFE is caused by excessive shearing forces at the proximal femoral physis (growth plate), resulting in displacement of the proximal femur diaphysis (neck) relative to the femoral epiphysis (head).  It is more common during adolescence when the physis is relatively weak due to its cartilaginous composition and rapid bone growth.  Patients who are obese are at higher risk for SCFE due to the increased mechanical strain.

Patients typically present with an antalgic gait (ie, altered posture/movement to minimize pain) and progressive hip pain exacerbated by activity.  Some patients may also have referred pain to the groin, thigh, or knee.  The affected hip is often held in external rotation; internal rotation is limited due to the displaced femoral neck impinging against the acetabulum.  Diagnosis is confirmed via x-ray showing anterosuperior displacement of the femoral neck, and management is surgical screw fixation.

(Choice A)  Septic arthritis involves bacterial invasion of the synovium and can present with joint pain that is worse with activity.  Unlike this patient, symptoms rapidly progress over days and include an erythematous, swollen joint and systemic symptoms (eg, fever, chills).

(Choice B)  Juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes degeneration and inflammation of the joint cartilage, leading to chronic pain and decreased range of motion of the affected joint.  In contrast to the findings seen in this patient, swelling and warmth of the joint would be expected, and monoarticular involvement of the hip would be unlikely.

(Choice D)  Stress-induced fracture of the cortical bone occurs as an overuse injury.  Pain worsens after activity but is typically focal, unlike this patient's groin and thigh pain.  In addition, pain with passive internal rotation of the hip is more consistent with articular pathology such as SCFE.

(Choice E)  Tendinopathy of the hip abductor muscles can cause an antalgic gait with pain aggravated by activity.  However, tenderness would be expected on the lateral, rather than the anterior, aspect of the hip.  Moreover, most patients are adults, making this diagnosis unlikely in this patient.

Educational objective:Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is due to excessive shearing forces that cause displacement of the femoral neck relative to the femoral head.  Risk factors include adolescence and obesity, and presentation typically involves progressive hip, thigh, groin, or knee pain with limited internal rotation of the affected hip.​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​
